## Purpose

This document demonstrates a complete workflow for Bayesian multilevel
analysis of sleepstudy data in R using brms, with prior specification,
posterior inference, and model diagnostics.

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE)
```

## Required packages

- **tidyverse:** Tools for importing, transforming, summarising, and
  visualising data.
- **knitr:** Executes R Markdown code chunks and formats tables and
  output.
- **brms:** Specifies Bayesian regression and multilevel models using an
  R formula interface.
- **rstan:** Interfaces with Stan to compile models and sample from
  posterior distributions.
- **loo:** Estimates out-of-sample predictive performance using
  approximate leave-one-out cross-validation.
- **bayesplot:** Visualises posterior draws, sampling diagnostics, and
  posterior predictive checks.
- **lme4:** Provides the sleepstudy dataset and fits frequentist
  mixed-effects models for comparison.

```{r packages}
library(brms)
library(rstan)
library(tidyverse)
library(bayesplot)
library(loo)
library(knitr)
library(lme4)
```

## 01 The sleepstudy warm-up

> How does RT change over days of sleep deprivation, and how
much do participants differ in their baseline RT and rate of
change?

We first fit a random-intercept model to establish the workflow, then
extend it to include participant-specific slopes.

```{r data}
data("sleepstudy", package = "lme4")
glimpse(sleepstudy)

# Look at the data first: one line per person
ggplot(sleepstudy, aes(Days, Reaction, group = Subject, colour = Subject)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.9, linewidth = 0.8) +
  labs(title = "Reaction time over days of sleep deprivation",
       x = "Days", y = "Reaction time (ms)") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

### Fit a simple model first

> How much does reaction time change per day, while accounting for participants 
having different starting reaction times?

```{r random-intercept-model}
# a collection of prior specifications
# Before updating with the observations, plausible values for the average RT
# level are distributed around 300 ms, with prior SD 100 ms.
priors_ri <- c(
  prior(normal(300, 100), class = Intercept), # Set the prior for the average level
  prior(normal(0, 10), class = b, coef = Days), # Set the prior for the slope of Days
  prior(student_t(3, 0, 50), class = sd), # Set the prior for the standard deviation of the random intercepts
  prior(student_t(3, 0, 50), class = sigma)# Set the prior for the residual standard deviation
)

# the fitted model object
m_brms_ri <- brms::brm(
  Reaction ~ Days + (1 | Subject), # Participants have different baseline RT,
                                   # but the same underlying daily change.
  data = sleepstudy,
  family = gaussian(), # Assume normally distributed variation around each expected RT.
  prior = priors_ri,
  backend = "rstan",
  iter = 2000,    # Total iterations per chain, including warmup
  warmup = 1000,  # Sampler adaptation; excluded from posterior summaries
  chains = 4,    # Four separate sampling chains
  cores = 2,     # Run up to two chains in parallel
  seed = 2026    # Reproducible random seed
)

summary(m_brms_ri)
plot(m_brms_ri)
pp_check(m_brms_ri, ndraws = 50) +
  labs(
    title = "Posterior predictive check",
    subtitle = "Observed reaction times (y) vs. 50 replicated datasets (y_rep)",
    x = "Reaction time (ms)",
    y = "Density"
  ) +
  yaxis_text(TRUE) +    # bayesplot hides the y-axis numbers by default
  yaxis_ticks(TRUE)
```
Under this random-intercept model and the specified priors, expected reaction time increases by about **10.41 ms/day**. The **95%** credible interval for the daily increase is **8.81–11.98 ms/day**.

The `pp_check()` function generates a probability density plot of the observed and replicated data. The plot shows two densities::
y: the estimated density of your observed 180 reaction times.
yrep: the estimated density of one replicated dataset generated from the fitted model.

The posterior predictive plot compares the observed reaction-time density (black, y) with the densities of 50 replicated datasets generated from the fitted model (blue, yrep). Broad agreement suggests that the model reproduces the overall outcome distribution, but does not establish that it captures individual trajectories.


```{r tighter-prior}
# Same priors as before, except for the Days slope
priors_tighter <- c(
  brms::set_prior("normal(300, 100)", class = "Intercept"),
  brms::set_prior("normal(0, 2)", class = "b", coef = "Days"), # a more concentrated prior
  brms::set_prior("student_t(3, 0, 50)", class = "sd"),
  brms::set_prior("student_t(3, 0, 50)", class = "sigma")
)

m_ri_tighter <- update(
  m_brms_ri,
  prior = priors_tighter,
  seed = 2026
)

# Compare the Days posterior
brms::fixef(m_brms_ri)["Days", ]
brms::fixef(m_ri_tighter)["Days", ]

summary(m_ri_tighter)
plot(m_ri_tighter)

pp_check(m_ri_tighter, ndraws = 50) +
  labs(
    title = "Posterior predictive check",
    subtitle = "Observed reaction times (y) vs. 50 replicated datasets (y_rep)",
    x = "Reaction time (ms)",
    y = "Density"
  ) +
  yaxis_text(TRUE) +    # bayesplot hides the y-axis numbers by default
  yaxis_ticks(TRUE)
```
Under the random-intercept model with the tighter slope prior, expected reaction time increases by approximately **8.94 ms/day**, with a **95%** credible interval of **7.38–10.49 ms/day**. The direction of the effect remained consistent, but its estimated magnitude was sensitive to the stronger zero-centred prior.
